Let x=e^u, y=e^v, and define g(t)=f(e^t). The equation becomes
\[
g(v+u)+g(v-u)=2\cosh(u)g(v) \qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R).\tag{1}
\]
Taking v=0 gives
\[
g(u)+g(-u)=2\cosh(u)g(0).
\]
Thus, with c=g(0), the function h(u)=g(u)-c\cosh u is odd and satisfies (1). We use the standard algebraic lemma: if an odd function h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R satisfies
\[
h(u+v)+h(v-u)=2\cosh(u)h(v),
\]
then h(u)=d\sinh u for some constant d. Indeed, writing the equation also with u and v interchanged and combining the resulting identities yields the sine-addition relation
\[
h(u+v)=h(u)\cosh v+h(v)\cosh u,
\]
and setting v=1, then using the same relation with arbitrary v and u+1, gives h(u)/\sinh u=h(1)/\sinh 1 for u\ne0; oddness handles u=0.
Therefore
\[
g(u)=c\cosh u+d\sinh u=Ae^u+Be^{-u}
\]
for suitable A,B\in\mathbb R. Returning to x=e^u,
\[
f(x)=Ax+\frac Bx.
\]
Conversely, direct substitution gives
\[
f(xy)+f(y/x)=Axy+\frac B{xy}+A\frac yx+B\frac xy
=\left(x+\frac1x\right)\left(Ay+\frac By\right),
\]
so every such function works. Hence all solutions are
\[
\boxed{f(x)=Ax+\frac Bx\quad(A,B\in\mathbb R).}
\]
outputs.reason: The original proof guessed the correct family but did not rigorously exclude other solutions; the logarithmic change of variables and an algebraic cosine-sine lemma complete the classification.
